clue.text: Between chest and hips, I wander endlessly between the sexes

indicators.note: something set between two things sits inside them, so the outer pair wraps the rest

parts.note: M for male and F for female, the two sexes as abbreviated on forms

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter of the verb is cut off

parts.note: taken as written
to drift is to wander aimlessly

explanation.surface: Someone describes their belly while musing on drifting between male and female identities.
explanation.walkthrough: I plus DRIF(t) sits between M and F.
explanation.definitionFit: The midriff is the middle region of the torso, below the ribcage and above the waist.

clue.text: Mooned from vehicle

definitions.meaning: first meaning: wandered about listlessly or sulked
second meaning: a light motorcycle with pedals

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mooned from vehicle' suggests baring a bottom from a car; 'mooned' is the dreamy, listless sense.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means drifted about listlessly or sulked, and as a noun it is a small low-powered motorbike.

clue.text: Uncertain if article right during homework

indicators.note: something happening during something else lies within it, so one string goes inside

parts.note: do-it-yourself, jobs done around the home
the definite article
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A student is unsure whether the essay is correct.
explanation.walkthrough: DI(THE R)Y. 'Homework' suggests school, but it is household DIY.
explanation.definitionFit: Dithery describes someone who hesitates and cannot make up their mind, so hesitant and unsure.

clue.text: Terrible chap in bed, topless

indicators.note: with no top, a down word loses its first letter

parts.note: a divan is a type of bed

explanation.surface: An awful man lies on a bed without his shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible' looks like a judgement, but it is the epithet of Ivan the Terrible, the Russian tsar.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivan IV of Russia is known in English as Ivan the Terrible, so he is the chap so described.

clue.text: As an Olympian, I threw up stout and I''m in need of a beer!

definitions.text: As an Olympian, I threw up

parts.note: stout means plump or fat
taken as written, without the apostrophe
taken as written
Whitbread is a long-established British brewer and its beer

explanation.surface: An athlete confesses to vomiting after stout and craving another pint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Threw up' and stout suggest a drinker being sick; the athlete threw the javelin up. Fatima Whitbread won Olympic javelin medals for Britain in 1984 and 1988.
explanation.definitionFit: Fatima Whitbread is a British javelin thrower who took Olympic bronze and silver medals in the 1980s.

clue.text: Where to find car in a state, having blown a gasket?

definitions.note: a phrase for a place standing in for a past-participle adjective

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for Georgia, a US state
to blow a gasket is to lose your temper, so raged

explanation.surface: A furious motorist is asked where the car went after an engine part failed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blown a gasket' looks mechanical, fitting the car, but it is the idiom for flying into a rage.
explanation.definitionFit: A car that is garaged is kept in its garage, so that is exactly where you would locate it.

clue.text: I can go in and serve almost entirely via annihilation — thus I won the championship!

indicators.note: annihilation destroys things completely, so the letters are wrecked and rebuilt
nearly all of the word is kept, losing just its final letter

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tennis champion boasts of serving opponents into annihilation on the way to the title.
explanation.walkthrough: Goran Ivanisevic, the big-serving Croat, won Wimbledon in 2001 as a wildcard, beating Pat Rafter in the final.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivanisevic won the 2001 Wimbledon men's singles title, the tennis championship the clue's speaker claims.

clue.text: Returning late from the pub carrying piano, something for evening out

indicators.note: carrying something means holding it, so the phrase wraps round the letter

parts.note: rolling in is arriving home late, often after drinking
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: A drunk staggers home with a piano after a night out.
explanation.walkthrough: ROLLING (P) IN. 'Evening out' reads as a night on the town, but means making pastry level.
explanation.definitionFit: A rolling pin is a kitchen cylinder used to flatten dough, making it smooth and even.

clue.text: Arm with head and a leg, but no tail, on part of ship

indicators.note: losing the tail means dropping the last letter of the phrase

parts.note: a gun is a firearm, an arm

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sailor with an arm, a head and a leg but no tail seems to be a pirate or merman aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with head' gives just W, and 'a leg' minus its tail gives ALE, another beer in this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: The gunwale is the upper edge of a boat's side, part of the hull's structure.

clue.text: "Indict beer", the talk of the local?

indicators.note: split off the front of the first word, this tells us one thing sits in the rest

parts.note: split as in plus dict, the word supplies the four letters after its first two
ale is beer

explanation.surface: A pub regular's quoted slogan sounds like a charge against beer.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is to split 'Indict' into two words, so its front half becomes the instruction. 'Local' suggests a pub but means a person from the area.
explanation.definitionFit: A dialect is the regional variety of speech used by people of one area, the locals.

clue.text: I was runner-up to 5 down — talk about service!

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: patter is glib, rapid talk
the RAF, the Royal Air Force, is one of the armed services

explanation.surface: A tennis finalist who lost reflects on the serving that decided the match.
explanation.walkthrough: PAT(RAF)TER. 'Service' suggests tennis serving, but it is the armed service. Pat Rafter lost the 2001 Wimbledon final to Goran Ivanisevic.
explanation.definitionFit: The Australian Pat Rafter was beaten finalist against Goran Ivanisevic in the 2001 Wimbledon men's final.

clue.text: A novice embraced by Asian flower, embraced by fat one, former glamour model

indicators.note: being embraced means being hugged inside, so the first pair goes within the river
the second hug puts that whole river-and-letters string inside the next words

parts.note: lard is pig fat
a flower here is something that flows, a river; the Indus is in Asia
taken as written
L for learner, from the plates on a learner driver's car
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A beginner is surrounded by an exotic bloom, all wrapped in something plump.
explanation.walkthrough: Two nested insertions: the novice pair goes into the river, and that goes into the fat between its first and second letters. 'Flower' reads as a bloom but is a river. Linda Lusardi was a 1980s British Page 3 model.
explanation.definitionFit: Linda Lusardi made her name as a British topless glamour model in the 1980s before turning to acting.

clue.text: Something done both ways

indicators.note: the word reads identically forwards and backwards, so it works in both directions

parts.note: a single act or action, which the clue adds reads the same either way

explanation.surface: A task is completed in two directions at once.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a palindrome, so the definition is given and then 'both ways' confirms the shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A deed is an act or action performed by someone, a thing that has been carried out.

clue.text: Free call-back in charge reversal by the crown

indicators.note: going back means the word is read from its end to its start

parts.note: to call someone something is to name them

indicators.note: the word itself tells us the preceding abbreviation is turned round

parts.note: i/c is the standard abbreviation for in charge
the pate is the crown of the head

explanation.surface: A phone call returned without cost leads to a reversal of power at the royal court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The crown' suggests monarchy, but here it is the top of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: To emancipate is to set free from slavery or legal restraint, so it serves as the verb free.

clue.text: Message about play, good for actor

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word surrounds the others

parts.note: a cable is a telegram, a message
to lark about is to play
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A telegram about a stage play praises it for an actor.
explanation.walkthrough: C(LARK G)ABLE. 'Play' suggests theatre but here it means fun.
explanation.definitionFit: Clark Gable was a Hollywood film star, best known for playing Rhett Butler in Gone with the Wind.

clue.text: Bordering principality virtually rejected local edict

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the shortened name is turned round

parts.note: Wales is formally a principality, its heir being the Prince of Wales

explanation.surface: A council in a region next to a small state throws out a by-law.
explanation.walkthrough: BY plus WALE(s) turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A byelaw is a regulation made by a local authority, applying only within its own area.

clue.text: Most questionable visitor invited to museum?

parts.note: the V and A, the Victoria and Albert Museum in London
a guest is a visitor

explanation.surface: Someone wonders which shady visitor got a museum invitation.
explanation.walkthrough: The museum comes first in the answer though last in the clue. The V&A is London's Victoria and Albert Museum.
explanation.definitionFit: Vaguest is the superlative of vague, meaning least clear and so most open to doubt.

clue.text: See 10
Have a cigarette and smile!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to ignite a cigarette and start smoking
second meaning: for a face to brighten with pleasure

explanation.surface: A cheerful order to relax with a smoke and grin.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to ignite tobacco and for one's face to become bright and happy.

clue.text: More bitter required, about a hundred — Brillo!

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: sourer is more bitter in taste
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A drinker at the bar demands a hundred more pints of bitter, crying brilliant!
explanation.walkthrough: S(C)OURER. Brillo is a brand of soap-filled wire pad, so 'Brillo!' is not British slang for brilliant here.
explanation.definitionFit: A Brillo pad is a brand of wire-wool pad for cleaning pans, a typical example of a scourer.

clue.text: Caught in denial, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps means the given word is only one possible form of the letters

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A suspect is trapped by a lie, perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Nailed is informal for caught or exposed, as when a culprit is nailed by the police.

clue.text: English books required in understanding narcissistic journey

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it

parts.note: a grip on something is an understanding of it
OT, the Old Testament books of the Bible

explanation.walkthrough: E + G(OT)RIP.
explanation.definitionFit: An ego trip is an activity done to boost self-importance, a self-centred indulgence like a vain journey.

clue.text: Footballer requesting King's bitter

explanation.walkthrough: Best bitter is the standard British ale style. George Best was a famous Manchester United footballer, noted for his drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: George Best was a Northern Irish winger for Manchester United, one of the great players of his era.

clue.text: I say "leave mum!"

parts.note: to go is to leave
mum means silent, and sh is the call for silence

explanation.surface: A child exclaims while being told to leave their mother alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' looks like mother, but here it means keep quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of surprise, and gosh is a stock British expression like I say.

clue.text: Run off with single member?

parts.note: surface reading: to flee or leave, the straight sense of the slangy command
setter's reading: moving away on just one leg, as when bounding on one foot

explanation.walkthrough: The British slang command to clear off is taken literally: going away using only one leg.
explanation.definitionFit: Hop it is a British slang order to go away, and hopping is moving on a single leg.

clue.text: In the Bible, Saul sold his birthright

parts.note: the last letter of one word and the start of the next

clue.text: Pulse demanded when making broth

parts.note: taken as written

clue.text: Earwig in sea proved to be floundering

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

clue.text: Threaten death by drink

death is the end

clue.text: A tasty bit of stuff for tea?

definitions.text: A tasty bit of stuff for tea

setter's reading: a toasted griddle cake eaten with butter at teatime
